learn.title: From average to instant
learn.body: The average rate uses two points. The instantaneous rate at one point asks what the average rate approaches as the second point slides toward the first. It is the slope of the tangent line, the line that just touches the curve there.

learn.title: The definition
learn.body: The derivative of $f$ at $a$ is $f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$. It is a limit of average rates over smaller and smaller intervals of width $h$.

learn.title: $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=3$
learn.body: Compute the average rate over width $h$.

learn.title: A pattern appears
learn.body: At $x=1$ the same steps give $2+h\to2$. At $x=3$ we got 6. The answers are $2x$, so the derivative of $x^2$ is $2x$. For a line like $3x+1$ the rate is always 3, since the slope never changes.

choices: The instantaneous rate of change at $x=a$

questions.prompt: For $f(x)=3x+1$, what is the instantaneous rate at any point?
questions.explanation: A line has the same slope everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which gets closer to an instantaneous rate?
choices: An average rate over a year
An average rate over a very short interval
questions.explanation: The shorter the interval, the closer to the instant.

questions.prompt: The slope of the tangent line at a point is the \_\_ there.
questions.explanation: That is the geometric meaning of $f'(a)$.
